passages.t: ‘In the shadow of Your wings’, and ‘I will awaken the dawn’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Miktam of David, when he fled from Saul into the cave” (verse 1). The prayer begins with a double cry. “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy, for in You my soul takes refuge. In the shadow of Your wings I will take shelter until the danger has passed” (verse 1).

He is among enemies like wild animals. “My soul is among the lions; I lie down with ravenous beasts” (verse 4). Between the danger and the praise comes a refrain: “Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth” (verses 5 and 11).

His enemies set a trap and fall into it themselves (verse 6). Then he sings. “My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast. I will sing and make music. Awake, my glory! Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awaken the dawn” (verses 7 and 8).
passages.hearers:
Two caves appear in David's story. He hid in the cave of Adullam with a band of men in trouble (1 Samuel 22:1). Later, near En-gedi by the Dead Sea, Saul walked alone into the very cave where David was hiding. David cut off a corner of Saul's robe but would not harm him (1 Samuel 24). The heading does not say which cave. Verse 6, where the hunters fall into their own pit, fits the En-gedi story well. The book page explains the headings.

‘The shadow of Your wings’ is the picture of a mother bird covering her young. Boaz used it of Ruth, who had come to trust Israel's God, “under whose wings you have taken refuge” (Ruth 2:12).

‘I will awaken the dawn’ is a lovely boast. Usually the dawn wakes the singer. Here the singer means to wake the dawn with praise.

Verses 7 to 11 appear again, almost word for word, as the start of Psalm 108.
passages.later:
Jesus used the wings picture of himself: “how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings” (Matthew 23:37).

David's refusal to harm Saul in the cave became a lesson in leaving revenge to God. Paul writes, “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath” (Romans 12:19).
passages.asks:
The psalm does not wait for the danger to pass before praising. The shelter is ‘until the danger has passed’. The praise starts in the cave.

‘My heart is steadfast’ means fixed, settled. Not calm because things are fine, but steady because God is. What would it look like for you to ‘awaken the dawn’ tomorrow, starting the day with praise while the trouble is still there?
